topicTitle: Concept of Health and Disease

images.alt: The Iceberg Phenomenon of Disease showing apparent clinical cases above the waterline and hidden subclinical disease below
images.caption: Iceberg of disease: clinical cases above the waterline and subclinical disease below.

images.alt: Levels of Prevention and Modes of Intervention mapped against the stages of disease progression
images.caption: Levels of prevention and modes of intervention mapped against stages of disease.
images.anchorText: Levels of Prevention & Modes of Intervention

images.alt: Health-sickness continuum from positive health through subclinical and clinical sickness to death
images.caption: Spectrum of health: a continuous gradient from positive health through better health, freedom from sickness, unrecognized sickness, mild sickness, and severe sickness, ending in death. A person moves along this line; there is no sharp cut between health and disease.

images.alt: Six core dimensions of health: physical, mental, social, spiritual, emotional, and vocational
images.caption: Dimensions of health: physical (organ function), mental (emotional balance and coping), social (community ties), spiritual (meaning and values), emotional (affective stability), and vocational (meaningful work). Other recognized dimensions include cultural, environmental, and nutritional.

images.alt: Multifactorial determinants of health: biological, behavioral, environmental, socio-economic, health system, demographic, and gender
images.caption: Determinants of health: biological (genes), behavioral and lifestyle, environmental, socio-economic (income, literacy, work), health system access, demographic structure, and gender. Health is the product of these interacting factors, not of medical care alone.

images.alt: Epidemiological triad of agent, host, and environment, with disease when equilibrium among the three is disrupted
images.caption: Epidemiological triad: disease arises when equilibrium among Agent, Host, and Environment is disrupted. Agents include biological, nutrient, physical, chemical, mechanical, and social forces. Host factors include age, sex, genes, and immunity. The environment brings agent and host together.

images.alt: Natural history of disease from prepathogenesis through subclinical and clinical pathogenesis to recovery, disability, or death, mapped to levels of prevention
images.caption: Natural history of disease. Prepathogenesis is the phase of susceptibility, before the agent enters the host; primordial and primary prevention apply here. Pathogenesis begins at entry, then subclinical change, clinical disease, and outcome (recovery, disability, or death). Secondary prevention is early diagnosis and treatment. Tertiary prevention is disability limitation and rehabilitation.

images.alt: Four evolving concepts of health: biomedical, ecological, psychosocial, and holistic
images.caption: Changing concepts of health: biomedical (absence of disease, germ theory), ecological (equilibrium with environment), psychosocial (health as a social and psychological phenomenon), and holistic (sound mind in a sound body, in a sound family, in a sound environment).

images.alt: Web of causation showing multiple interacting agent, host, and environmental factors rather than a single cause
images.caption: Web of causation: most diseases arise from interacting agent, host, and environmental factors, not from a single germ. Pettenkofer argued for multifactorial causation. Breaking any sufficient strand in the web can prevent disease.

topicTitle: Epidemiological Methods, Descriptive Epidemiology, and Disease Fluctuations

images.alt: Hierarchy of Epidemiological Evidence showing study designs from weakest to strongest
images.caption: Hierarchy of epidemiological evidence, from weakest designs at the base to strongest at the top.

images.alt: Three epidemic curve patterns: point-source, continuous common-source, and propagated person-to-person spread
images.caption: Time distribution of epidemics. A point-source outbreak rises and falls in a single peak within one incubation period. A continuous common-source outbreak has a drawn-out downslope or extra peaks while exposure continues. A propagated outbreak rises gradually with successive waves about one incubation period apart.

images.alt: Steps in investigation of an epidemic from verifying diagnosis through time-place-person analysis and hypothesis testing
images.caption: Investigation of an epidemic: verify the diagnosis, confirm that incidence exceeds the endemic baseline, define the population at risk, search actively for cases, analyse time, place, and person, form hypotheses about source and route, then test them.

images.alt: Indian vaccine cold chain from state WIC/WIF through district and PHC ILRs to sub-centre vaccine carriers
images.caption: Cold chain in India: state WIC/WIF holds 3 months of stock; district and PHC ILR/DF hold 1 month; sub-centre vaccine carriers last 24 to 48 hours. Failure risk is highest at session sites.
images.anchorText: COLD CHAIN HIERARCHY AND VULNERABILITIES IN INDIA

images.alt: Shake test comparing a suspect aluminium-adsorbed vaccine vial with a frozen-thawed control to detect freeze damage
images.caption: Shake test: used for aluminium-adsorbed freeze-sensitive vaccines (DPT, Td, TT, Hepatitis B, pentavalent, PCV). Shake a suspect vial and a frozen-thawed control from the same batch for 10 to 15 seconds, then watch sedimentation for 30 minutes. Pass: the suspect vial stays cloudy longer than the control. Fail: the suspect vial sediments as fast as or faster than the control; discard it.

images.alt: Open vial policy allowing 28-day reuse of liquid multi-dose vaccines with preservative, excluding reconstituted live vaccines
images.caption: Open vial policy (2015): opened liquid multi-dose vials with preservative (bOPV, IPV, pentavalent, Hep B, DPT, Td, TT, liquid PCV) may be reused for 28 days if expiry, +2 to +8 C, clean septum, aseptic withdrawal, and VVM are all acceptable. Reconstituted BCG, measles/MR, JE and rotavirus are excluded; discard within 4 hours (2 hours for JE) or at session end.

topicTitle: Respiratory Infections - Part A (Smallpox, Mpox, Chickenpox, Measles, Rubella, Mumps, Diphtheria, Pertussis)

images.alt: Measles clinical course from incubation through prodrome with Koplik spots, downward-spreading rash, and key complications
images.caption: Measles clinical course: about 10 days to fever and 14 days to rash. The 4-day prodrome brings coryza, cough, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots. The dusky-red rash starts behind the ears and spreads downward. Infectious period is 4 days before to 4 days after the rash.

images.alt: Side-by-side comparison of smallpox and chickenpox rash distribution, depth, and evolution
images.caption: Smallpox rash is centrifugal, deep-seated, and all lesions are at the same stage; palms and soles are often involved. Chickenpox rash is centripetal, superficial, appears in crops, and lesions at different stages coexist; palms and soles are usually spared.

topicTitle: Intestinal Infections - Part A (Poliomyelitis, Viral Hepatitis A, B, C, D, E)

images.alt: Polio clinical spectrum from inapparent infection through abortive illness, non-paralytic meningitis, and paralytic disease
images.caption: Polio clinical spectrum: 91 to 96 percent of infections are inapparent. About 4 to 8 percent are abortive minor illness. About 1 percent is non-paralytic (aseptic meningitis). Less than 1 percent is paralytic, with asymmetrical flaccid paralysis and no sensory loss.

images.alt: Comparison of hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E by route, incubation, chronicity, and vaccine
images.caption: Hepatitis A and E spread faecal-orally and do not become chronic; E is dangerous in pregnancy. Hepatitis B, C, and D spread parenterally; B and C can become chronic. D needs B. Vaccines exist for A and B (and therefore D). Incubation is shortest for A and E, longest for B.

images.alt: Natural history of hepatitis B from acute infection through chronic carriage to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
images.caption: Hepatitis B: after acute infection, most adults recover and become immune (anti-HBs). A minority become chronic HBsAg carriers; risk is highest if infection is acquired at birth. Chronic infection can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Vaccine and birth-dose plus HBIG for exposed newborns prevent this path.

topicTitle: Arthropod-Borne Infections (Dengue Syndrome, Malaria, Lymphatic Filariasis, Zika Virus)

images.alt: Malaria life cycle showing human hepatic and erythrocytic schizogony and mosquito sporogony from gametocyte to salivary sporozoite
images.caption: Malaria life cycle. In humans, sporozoites start hepatic schizogony (hypnozoites in P. vivax and P. ovale), then erythrocytic schizogony. Gametocytes infect the mosquito. Sporogony runs gametocyte to zygote, ookinete, oocyst, then salivary-gland sporozoites.

images.alt: Dengue clinical ladder from undifferentiated fever through classical dengue fever, dengue haemorrhagic fever, and dengue shock syndrome
images.caption: Dengue clinical ladder: undifferentiated fever, classical dengue fever (break-bone pain, retro-orbital pain, biphasic fever, rash), dengue haemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage, and dengue shock syndrome. Secondary infection with a different serotype can trigger antibody-dependent enhancement.

images.alt: Life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti between human definitive host and Culex mosquito intermediate host
images.caption: Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti in India): humans are the definitive host; Culex quinquefasciatus is the intermediate host and vector. Microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity. The mosquito takes up microfilariae, which develop to infective larvae, then are deposited on skin during a later bite.

topicTitle: Zoonoses (Rabies, Yellow Fever, Japanese Encephalitis, Rickettsial Zoonoses)

images.alt: Rabies pathogenesis from bite-site replication through centripetal nerve spread to the CNS and centrifugal spread to salivary glands
images.caption: Rabies pathogenesis: virus replicates near the bite, travels centripetally along peripheral nerves to the CNS, then spreads centrifugally to salivary glands and other tissues. Clinical picture includes prodrome, hydrophobia, aerophobia, and spasms.

images.alt: Japanese encephalitis zoonotic cycle with ardeid birds, pigs as amplifiers, Culex tritaeniorhynchus, and humans as dead-end hosts
images.caption: Japanese encephalitis: Culex tritaeniorhynchus (and related rice-field Culex) transmit JE virus. Ardeid birds are the natural reservoir. Pigs are amplifying hosts. Humans and horses are dead-end hosts; they do not infect mosquitoes. Incubation is about 5 to 15 days.

topicTitle: Surface Infections - Part A (Tetanus, Leprosy)

images.alt: Leprosy Ridley-Jopling immuno-histological spectrum from TT to LL mapped onto WHO paucibacillary and multibacillary classes
images.caption: Leprosy spectrum. Ridley-Jopling runs TT, BT, BB, BL, LL according to cell-mediated immunity. WHO control classes: paucibacillary (1 to 5 skin lesions, one nerve, smear negative) and multibacillary (6 or more lesions, more than one nerve, or any positive smear).

images.alt: Tetanus wound prophylaxis combining wound care, tetanus toxoid, and TIG according to immunization status and wound type
images.caption: After injury: clean the wound. Completely immunized people (3 or more TT doses, last dose within 5 years) need no booster for clean wounds; a booster if the last dose was more than 5 years ago for dirty wounds, or more than 10 years for clean wounds, depending on Park/NIS tables. Unimmunized or unknown status: TT plus TIG for dirty/tetanus-prone wounds. TIG is passive; TT is active.

topicTitle: Surface Infections - Part B (STDs, HIV/AIDS) & 5.6 Emerging/Re-emerging Infections & 5.7 Hospital Acquired Infections

images.alt: WHO clinical staging of HIV disease from asymptomatic stage 1 through opportunistic infections of stage 4
images.caption: WHO clinical staging of HIV: Stage 1 asymptomatic or persistent generalized lymphadenopathy. Stage 2 moderate weight loss under 10 percent, zoster, recurrent respiratory infection. Stage 3 severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, oral candidiasis, pulmonary TB. Stage 4 AIDS-defining illness including PCP, extra-pulmonary TB, and HIV wasting.
images.anchorText: WHO CLINICAL STAGING OF HIV DISEASE

topicTitle: Coronary Heart Disease, Hypertension, Stroke, and Rheumatic Heart Disease

images.alt: Pathogenesis of rheumatic heart disease from Group A streptococcal pharyngitis through acute rheumatic fever to chronic valvular damage, with Jones criteria
images.caption: Rheumatic heart disease pathogenesis: untreated Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, molecular mimicry with cardiac myosin, acute rheumatic fever 2 to 3 weeks later in 1 to 3 percent of untreated cases, then cumulative valvular damage after recurrences. Jones diagnosis needs evidence of preceding GAS plus 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, manifestations.

images.alt: Coronary heart disease pathway from atherosclerotic risk factors to angina, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmia, and sudden death
images.caption: Coronary heart disease: obstructive atherosclerotic change in coronary arteries produces a mismatch between myocardial blood supply and demand. Clinical outcomes are angina, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death. South Asian onset is about a decade earlier than in Western cohorts.

topicTitle: Environment and Health: Waste & Excreta Disposal

images.alt: F-diagram of faecal-oral transmission through fingers, flies, fields, fluids, fomites and food, with primary and secondary sanitation barriers
images.caption: F-diagram: faecal pathogens reach a new host through fingers, flies, fields, fluids, fomites, and food. The primary barrier is isolation of excreta at the latrine. Secondary barriers are safe water, food hygiene, fly control, and handwashing with soap.

topicTitle: Entomology: Vectors & Disease Transmission

images.alt: Three modes of biological transmission in arthropods: cyclo-developmental, propagative, and cyclo-propagative, with classic examples
images.caption: Biological transmission inside the arthropod. Cyclo-developmental: development without multiplication (Wuchereria in Culex). Propagative: multiplication without cyclical change (Yersinia in the rat flea; dengue and yellow fever viruses in Aedes). Cyclo-propagative: both development and multiplication (Plasmodium in Anopheles).

topicTitle: Contraceptive Methods Part 2: Hormonal and Non-Hormonal Methods

images.alt: Mechanism of combined oral contraceptives and progestogen-only pills on GnRH, FSH, LH, cervical mucus, and endometrium
images.caption: Combined oral pills suppress ovulation by negative feedback on hypothalamic GnRH, blocking pituitary FSH and LH. Secondary actions thicken cervical mucus and alter the endometrium. Progestogen-only pills mainly thicken mucus, slow tubal transport, and desynchronize the endometrium.
images.anchorText: MECHANISM OF ACTION OF ORAL PILLS

topicTitle: Experimental Epidemiology, Causation, and Uses of Epidemiology

images.alt: Nine Bradford Hill criteria for causal inference, with temporality as the indispensable criterion
images.caption: Bradford Hill criteria (1965) for judging whether an association is causal: temporality (the only indispensable criterion), strength, dose-response, consistency, specificity, biological plausibility, coherence, experiment, and analogy.
images.anchorText: BRADFORD HILL CRITERIA FOR CAUSAL INFERENCE

images.alt: Six sequential steps of a randomized controlled trial from protocol through outcome assessment
images.caption: RCT steps: (1) drawing up the protocol, (2) selecting reference and experimental populations, (3) randomization, (4) manipulation or intervention, (5) follow-up, (6) assessment of outcome. Randomization is the heart of the trial and balances known and unknown confounders.
images.anchorText: STEPS OF A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL

topicTitle: Introduction, Tools of Measurement, and Measurement of Morbidity & Mortality

images.alt: Steady-state relationship P equals I times D linking prevalence, incidence, and mean duration of disease
images.caption: In a steady population, point prevalence equals incidence times mean duration (P = I x D). Incidence reflects new cases. Duration reflects how long people remain diseased. Prevalence rises if incidence rises or if people live longer with the disease.

topicTitle: Concepts, Levels, and Delivery Models of Health Care

images.alt: Three levels of health care in India from Ayushman Arogya Mandir and PHC through CHC and district hospital to tertiary centres
images.caption: Levels of health care. Primary care is first contact at Sub-centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) and PHCs. Secondary care is first referral at CHCs and district hospitals. Tertiary care is superspecialty at medical colleges and regional institutes.

images.alt: Eight essential elements of primary health care from the Alma-Ata declaration plus four principles
images.caption: Alma-Ata primary health care has eight essential elements: education, nutrition, safe water and sanitation, MCH including family planning, immunization, prevention and control of endemic diseases, treatment of common diseases and injuries, and essential drugs. Four principles: equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination, and appropriate technology.

topicTitle: Introduction, Maternity Cycle, Antenatal, Intranatal, and Postnatal Care

images.alt: Five-phase maternity cycle from fertilization through antenatal, intranatal, postnatal, and inter-conceptional periods
images.caption: Maternity cycle: fertilization in the tubal ampulla, antenatal (prenatal) period, intranatal period, postnatal period, then the inter-conceptional interval. Implantation in the endometrium occurs 8 to 10 days after fertilization.
images.anchorText: MATERNITY CYCLE AND PERIODS OF GROWTH

topicTitle: Accidents, Injuries, Haddon Matrix, and Snakebite Envenoming

images.alt: Haddon matrix 3-by-3 grid of host, vector or agent, and environment across pre-event, event, and post-event phases
images.caption: Haddon matrix: a 3-by-3 grid that crosses the epidemiological triad (host, vector or agent, physical and socioeconomic environment) with time (pre-event, event, post-event) to plan injury prevention.

topicTitle: Growth Charts, Low Birth Weight, Prematurity, and Kangaroo Mother Care

images.alt: Road to Health weight-for-age growth chart with direction of growth and reference curves
images.caption: Growth chart (Road to Health): a weight-for-age plot for infants and young children. Weight falls first in undernutrition. India uses sex-specific charts on the Mother and Child Protection card (blue for boys, pink for girls).

images.alt: Kangaroo mother care with prolonged skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding, early discharge, and follow-up for LBW infants
images.caption: Kangaroo mother care for low-birth-weight infants: prolonged skin-to-skin contact between baby and mother (or father), exclusive breastfeeding, early discharge with support, and close follow-up. It keeps the infant warm, supports feeding, and reduces infection and mortality.

topicTitle: Analytical Epidemiology: Case Control, Cohort, Cross-Sectional, and Ecological Studies

images.alt: Case-control studies look backward from disease to exposure; cohort studies look forward from exposure to disease
images.caption: Case-control studies start with diseased and non-diseased people and look backward to exposure; they give an odds ratio. Cohort studies start with exposed and unexposed people who are disease-free and follow them forward; they give incidence and relative risk.
images.anchorText: DIFFERENCES BETWEEN CASE-CONTROL AND COHORT STUDIES

topicTitle: Infectious Disease Epidemiology, Transmission Dynamics, and Disease Control

images.alt: Direct and indirect modes of disease transmission including contact, droplet, inoculation, soil, vertical, and vehicle routes
images.caption: Modes of transmission. Direct: physical contact, droplet spray under 1 metre, inoculation, contact with soil, and vertical (transplacental) spread. Indirect routes include vehicles such as the classic environmental 5 Fs.
images.anchorText: CLASSIFICATION OF MODES OF DISEASE TRANSMISSION

images.alt: Classification of carriers by clinical phase, duration of shedding, and portal of exit
images.caption: Carriers shed pathogen without current illness, or after it. By phase: incubatory, convalescent, healthy (asymptomatic). By duration: temporary versus chronic (for example Salmonella Typhi, hepatitis B). Chronic carriers keep disease endemic.

images.alt: Isolation separates infected people during communicability; quarantine restricts healthy contacts during the longest incubation period
images.caption: Isolation separates infected persons or animals during the period of communicability. Quarantine restricts healthy contacts of a case for the longest usual incubation period. Isolation is for the sick; quarantine is for the well who were exposed.

images.alt: Herd immunity as group resistance that blocks chains of transmission once a threshold of immune people is reached
images.caption: Herd immunity is the resistance of a group to invasion and spread of an infectious agent because a large proportion of members are immune. Transmission chains break when the immune fraction exceeds about 1 minus 1/R0. It protects remaining susceptibles, including people who cannot be vaccinated.

topicTitle: Respiratory Infections - Part B (Influenza, Acute Respiratory Infections, Pneumonia, Tuberculosis)

images.alt: Natural history of tuberculosis from droplet-nucleus exposure through latent infection to active disease and onward transmission
images.caption: Natural history of tuberculosis: inhalation of droplet nuclei from a sputum-positive case leads to infection (tuberculin conversion in 3 to 6 weeks). About 90 percent of infected people contain the bacilli as latent infection. Five to 10 percent develop clinical disease in a lifetime. An untreated infectious pulmonary case can infect 10 to 15 people in a year. Effective treatment cuts infectivity by about 90 percent within 48 hours. HIV is the strongest risk factor for progression from infection to disease.

images.alt: IMCI classification of cough or difficult breathing in children 2 months to 5 years by danger signs, chest indrawing, and fast breathing
images.caption: IMCI (2 months to 5 years): cough or difficult breathing. Severe pneumonia or very severe disease: any general danger sign, chest indrawing, or stridor in a calm child. Pneumonia: fast breathing. No pneumonia: cough or cold. Fast breathing is 50 or more per minute at 2 to 12 months, and 40 or more at 12 months to 5 years.

images.alt: Antigenic shift as major reassortment causing pandemics versus antigenic drift as gradual mutation causing seasonal epidemics
images.caption: Influenza A surface antigens are haemagglutinin and neuraminidase. Antigenic drift is gradual point mutation and causes seasonal epidemics. Antigenic shift is sudden reassortment of gene segments, can create a novel subtype, and causes pandemics (1918, 1957, 1968). Only influenza A undergoes shift.

topicTitle: Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity, Physical Activity, and WHO STEPS

images.alt: WHO STEPS NCD risk-factor surveillance with questionnaire, physical measurements, and biochemistry
images.caption: WHO STEPS is stepwise NCD risk-factor surveillance. Step 1 is a questionnaire (tobacco, alcohol, diet, physical activity, history). Step 2 is physical measurements (blood pressure, height, weight, waist). Step 3 is biochemistry (fasting glucose, lipids, optional urine). Each country can stop after the step it can afford, but all three give a full risk profile.
images.anchorText: WHO STEPwise APPROACH TO NCD RISK FACTOR SURVEILLANCE (STEPS)

topicTitle: Cancers: Epidemiology, Downstaging, and Cervical Cancer Elimination

images.alt: Cancer downstaging as detection at an earlier clinical stage through awareness and simple screening, illustrated with cervical cancer
images.caption: Downstaging of cancer means finding the disease at an earlier clinical stage, when treatment works better. It uses awareness of early signs plus simple tests (for cervix: VIA/VILI or HPV testing and cytology). It is not the same as preventing the first cancer cell; it shifts stage at diagnosis downward.

topicTitle: Contraceptive Methods Part 1: Spacing Methods and Intra-Uterine Devices

images.alt: Classification of contraceptive methods into spacing and terminal methods with major spacing subgroups
images.caption: Contraceptive methods: spacing (barrier, IUDs, hormonal, natural/traditional) and terminal (male and female sterilization). Spacing methods are reversible. Terminal methods are intended to be permanent. Cafeteria choice means the couple picks from the available range.

images.alt: Copper IUD mechanism: sterile inflammatory reaction in the uterus that is spermicidal and impairs implantation
images.caption: Copper IUDs (for example CuT 380A) act mainly before fertilization: copper ions and a sterile uterine inflammatory reaction are spermicidal and impair sperm and ovum. They also make the endometrium hostile to implantation. They do not work as abortifacients in the clinical sense used in Park. CuT 380A is approved for 10 years.

topicTitle: Breastfeeding, Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative, and Artificial Feeding

images.alt: Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding of the Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative
images.caption: Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative uses the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding: written policy, staff training, antenatal information, early skin-to-skin and initiation, show mothers how, no food or drink other than breast milk unless indicated, rooming-in, cue-based feeding, no teats or pacifiers, and discharge support including community groups.

topicTitle: Intestinal Infections - Part B (Acute Diarrhoeal Diseases, Cholera, Typhoid Fever, Food Poisoning, Amoebiasis, Helminthiasis)

images.alt: Typhoid pathogenesis from faecal-oral ingestion through Peyer patches to bacteraemia and chronic gallbladder carriage
images.caption: Typhoid (Salmonella Typhi): faecal-oral ingestion, invasion of Peyer patches, then bacteraemia (step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia). Complications include haemorrhage and perforation in the third week. A chronic carrier state, often gallbladder, can persist. Incubation is usually 10 to 14 days.

images.alt: Cholera rice-water stools and WHO dehydration treatment plans A, B, and C
images.caption: Cholera (Vibrio cholerae O1/O139) causes painless rice-water stools and rapid dehydration. WHO Plan A is home ORS for no dehydration, Plan B is ORS on-site for some dehydration, Plan C is IV Ringer lactate for severe dehydration. Zinc in children. Prevention: safe water, sanitation, and vaccination in outbreaks.

topicTitle: Plague, Leptospirosis, Kyasanur Forest Disease, and Nipah

images.alt: Plague cycle of Yersinia pestis with rodent reservoir, Xenopsylla cheopis flea, and proventricular blockage, not salivary transmission
images.caption: Plague (Yersinia pestis): wild and commensal rodents are the reservoir. The classic vector is the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis. After a blood meal, bacilli block the proventriculus; the starving flea regurgitates bacilli into the next bite. This is not salivary-gland transmission. Urban cycle: Rattus rattus / R. norvegicus to flea to humans.

topicTitle: Blindness, Deafness, Disability Rights, and Pesticide Genetic Effects

images.alt: WHO versus NPCB definitions of blindness by presenting visual acuity
images.caption: WHO blindness is presenting visual acuity worse than 3/60 in the better eye. NPCB (India) uses worse than 6/60 in the better eye for programme blindness. Low vision sits between 6/18 and the blindness cut-off. Cataract is the leading avoidable cause in India.

topicTitle: Mortality Indicators: Maternal, Perinatal, Neonatal, Infant, and Child Mortality

images.alt: Maternal death surveillance and response cycle from identification through response and monitoring
images.caption: Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) is a continuous cycle: identify and notify every maternal death, review the medical and social causes, analyse findings, respond with actions that prevent similar deaths, and monitor that the actions happened. It is surveillance for action, not a blame exercise.
